title: International atomic clock comparison achieving $5\times 10^{-18}$ uncertainty
authors: A. Tofful, M. Filzinger, T. Schmidt, A. Amy-Klein, E. Benkler, E. Cantin, C. Chardonnet, E. A. Curtis, H. Denker, B. Dutta, J. -O. Gaudron, W. Huang, J. Kronjäger, A. Kuhl, R. Le Targat, B. Lipphardt, O. Lopez, S. Mukherjee, A. L. Parke, B. Pointard, P. -E. Pottie, P. J. Regan, M. Risaro, M. Schioppo, M. Steinel, J. Tunesi, X. Zhang, R. M. Godun, N. Huntemann
abstract: Two single-ion optical clocks, located in the United Kingdom and in Germany, are compared remotely via a 2220\,km long optical fiber link. Both clocks are based on the ${}^2S_{1/2} (F=0)\leftrightarrow {}^2F_{7/2} (F=3)$ electric octupole (E3) transition in $^{171}\text{Yb}^+$. Using more than $10^6$ seconds of measurement data, we determine a fractional frequency difference of $1.0(4.8)\times 10^{-18}$, demonstrating agreement of the independently developed systems. To our knowledge, this constitutes the first international clock comparison reaching a fractional uncertainty below $5\times 10^{-18}$, an important milestone towards an anticipated optical redefinition of the SI second. The measurement uncertainty is dominated by that of the relativistic redshift correction between the two sites, which includes time-varying gravity potential differences. We exploit the large baseline between the two clocks to search for violations of Lorentz invariance. In the absence of statistically significant modulations, we improve constraints on the Robertson-Mansouri-Sexl parameter $α$ by approximately a factor of five in the uncertainty, and provide limits on corresponding parameters within the Standard-Model Extension framework.
summary: Researchers compared two state-of-the-art single-ion optical clocks over a long-distance fiber link, achieving an unprecedented frequency stability of $10^{-18}$. This milestone not only advances the goal of redefining the SI second but also allows for highly sensitive tests of fundamental physics, constraining potential violations of Lorentz invariance.
main_problem: To achieve the highest possible precision in international atomic clock comparisons and test fundamental physics symmetries like Lorentz invariance.
main_result: The comparison achieved a fractional frequency uncertainty of $1.0(4.8) 	imes 10^{-18}$, setting a new benchmark for international clock comparisons. They also significantly improved constraints on Lorentz violation parameters.
method: Remote comparison of two single-ion optical clocks using a long-baseline optical fiber link, combined with rigorous systematic error analysis.
model_or_system: The system involves two single-ion optical clocks based on the electric octupole (E3) transition in the ${}^{171}	ext{Yb}^+$ ion. The comparison is performed over a $2220 	ext{ km}$ fiber link, requiring careful correction for relativistic redshift differences.
